before: Under US law, individuals who acquire nationality of an E-2 treaty country through financial investment may be subject to a three-year continuous domicile requirement before qualifying under that nationality.
after: Under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(E), individuals who acquired the relevant treaty-country nationality through financial investment and have not previously been granted E status must demonstrate at least three continuous years of domicile in that country at some point before applying. Turkish passport ownership alone does not satisfy that requirement.

before: One of the most important developments affecting citizenship-by-investment planning is the three-year domicile rule introduced through US legislation enacted in 2022.
after: One of the most important developments affecting citizenship-by-investment planning is the three-year domicile rule introduced by section 5902(b) of Public Law 117-263, enacted on December 23, 2022.

before: Under the relevant statutory framework, qualifying applicants may need to demonstrate that they have been continuously domiciled in the treaty country for at least three years before seeking E-2 eligibility based on that nationality.
after: Under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(E), the requirement applies to applicants who acquired the relevant nationality through financial investment and have not previously been granted E status. They must establish a continuous period of at least three years of domicile in the treaty country, completed at some point before applying. The statute does not say that the period must fall immediately before the application.

before: Any statutory exceptions and transitional provisions must also be evaluated.
after: The statutory qualification concerning people previously granted E status must be evaluated individually. Acquiring a passport before December 23, 2022 is not, by itself, an exemption stated in the amendment.

before: A person's actual residence and domicile history may be legally relevant.
after: A person's actual residence and domicile history may be legally relevant. The statute does not expressly say that the entire qualifying period must follow nationality acquisition; that wording should not be treated as a guarantee that a particular pre-naturalization period will be accepted.

before: Domicile is a legal concept associated with a person's principal home and intention to maintain it.
after: Domicile generally concerns a person's principal home and intention to maintain it. Section 5902(b) does not supply a detailed E-visa domicile definition or evidence checklist, so this general explanation is not a definitive test for an individual application.

before: An investor should evaluate the proposed US business, source and commitment of funds, ownership or control structure, commercial viability and applicable visa requirements.
after: An investor should evaluate the proposed US business, lawful source and at-risk commitment of funds, ownership or operational control, commercial viability and applicable visa requirements. The enterprise must be real and operating and must not be marginal under the E-2 standard. The applicant must intend to depart when E status ends.

before: The applicable procedure depends on the applicant's circumstances and whether the application involves consular visa processing or another available immigration procedure.
after: The applicable procedure depends on the applicant's circumstances. Consular visa issuance and an eligible change of status through USCIS are different procedures; a change of status in the United States does not itself issue a visa for future travel.

before: Mainland China is not generally treated as an E-2 treaty country for this purpose, whereas Turkey has E-2 treaty status.
after: Mainland China does not have E-2 treaty coverage on the State Department list, whereas Turkey does. The list's separate China (Taiwan) entry must not be treated as coverage for mainland Chinese nationality.

before: China generally does not recognize dual nationality for Chinese nationals, and acquisition of foreign nationality may have significant consequences under Chinese law.
after: Article 3 of China's Nationality Law does not recognize dual nationality for Chinese nationals. Under Article 9, a Chinese national who has settled abroad and voluntarily acquires foreign nationality loses Chinese nationality automatically; the statutory conditions and the individual's circumstances require Chinese-law advice.

before: India does not generally recognize dual citizenship in the conventional sense.
after: Under section 9 of India's Citizenship Act 1955, voluntary acquisition of another citizenship generally terminates Indian citizenship, subject to the Act's provisions. Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) is not Indian citizenship.
